content: 1. The Cardiovascular Health Study demonstrated a significant association between physical function and mortality in older adults. This study highlights the importance of maintaining physical health to improve survival outcomes. (J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci, 2010; 65(1):63–70). 2. Ritchie et al. found that unintentional weight loss in community-dwelling older adults predicts a decline in activities of daily living (ADL) and life-space mobility over a four-year period. This underscores the need for early intervention in cases of unexplained weight loss. (J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci, 2008; 63(1):67–75). 3. Rothman et al. explored the prognostic significance of potential frailty criteria, emphasizing the need for early identification and management of frailty to improve health outcomes in older adults. (J Am Geriatr Soc, 2008; 56(12):2211–6). 4. Beydoun and Popkin investigated the impact of socioeconomic factors on functional status decline among older adults in China, revealing that lower socioeconomic status is a significant risk factor for functional deterioration. (Soc Sci Med, 2005; 60(9):2045–57). 5. Milne et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, showing that protein and energy supplementation in malnourished elderly individuals can improve nutritional status and reduce the risk of adverse health outcomes. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2009; (2):CD003288). 6. Baldwin and Weekes evaluated the effectiveness of dietary advice, with or without oral nutritional supplements, for disease-related malnutrition in adults. Their findings suggest that tailored nutritional interventions can improve clinical outcomes. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2011; 9:CD002008). 7. Munk et al. demonstrated that individualized dietary counseling for nutritionally at-risk older patients after hospital discharge significantly improves nutritional and functional outcomes. (J Hum Nutr Diet, 2016; 29(2):196–208). 8. Aleman-Mateo et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial showing that protein-rich food supplementation in sarcopenic elderly men not only increases muscle mass but also has additional physiological benefits. (Clin Interv Aging, 2012; 7:225–34). 9. De Jong et al. examined the effects of dietary supplements and physical exercise on sensory perception, appetite, dietary intake, and body weight in frail elderly individuals, highlighting the combined benefits of nutrition and exercise. (Br J Nutr, 2000; 83(6):605–13). 10. Gray-Donald et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial that found limited effects of nutritional supplementation on functional status among free-living frail elderly individuals, suggesting the need for more targeted interventions. (J Nutr, 1995; 125(12):2965–71). 11. Hampson et al. investigated the effects of dietary improvement on bone metabolism in underweight elderly women with osteoporosis, demonstrating significant benefits in bone health. (Osteoporos Int, 2003; 14(9):750–6). 12. Kim and Lee found that protein-energy supplementation can prevent functional decline in frail older adults with low socioeconomic status, emphasizing the importance of community-based nutritional interventions. (J Gerontology, 2013; 68(3):309–16). 13. Kim et al. conducted a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial showing that exercise combined with milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) supplementation improves body composition, physical function, and hematological parameters in frail Japanese women. (PLoS One, 2015; 10(2):e0116256). 14. McMurdo et al. evaluated whether oral nutritional supplementation should be provided to undernourished older adults upon hospital discharge, finding improvements in muscle strength and overall health outcomes. (J Am Geriatr Soc, 2009; 57(12):2239–45). 15. Payette et al. demonstrated the benefits of nutritional supplementation in free-living, frail, undernourished elderly individuals, showing improvements in weight and functional status. (J Am Diet Assoc, 2002; 102(8):1088–95). 16. Scorer investigated the effects of nutritional supplementation with Ensure on the general health of undernourished elderly patients in the community, finding significant improvements in nutritional status. (Clin Nutr, 2004; 23(2):195–204). 17. Tieland et al. showed that protein supplementation improves physical performance in frail elderly individuals in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. (J Am Med Dir Assoc, 2012; 13(8):720–6). 18. Uster et al. found that nutritional interventions improve dietary intake and quality of life in cancer patients, emphasizing the importance of addressing malnutrition in this population. (Nutrition, 2013; 29(11–12):1342–9). 19. Yamaguchi et al. demonstrated that liquid nutritional supplementation improves nutrient intake in elderly Meals-on-Wheels participants, particularly those with inadequate dietary intake. (Nutr Today, 1998; 33(1):37–44). 20. Bonnefoy et al. investigated the effects of exercise and protein-energy supplements on body composition and muscle function in frail elderly individuals, showing long-term benefits in physical health. (Br J Nutr, 2003; 89(5):731–9).
